data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy": null, "claim": "Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference to truth, but as a methodological rule for selecting the most 'testable' (and thus most informative) target for future falsification; however, this defense survives only by accepting that scientific action relies on a pragmatic leap where 'best available' substitutes for 'probable,' effectively costing the system any claim to rational assurance of success in practical application.", "counterconditions": [{"case": "If verisimilitude (truth-likeness) is required to justify action, the argument fails because Tichý and Miller demonstrated Popper's formal definition of verisimilitude is logically incoherent for comparing false theories.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If the preference implies any probability increase based on past survival, it smuggles in the very induction Popper rejected.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If the normative justification for action cannot be separated from the descriptive fact of survival, the analogy to natural selection collapses.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}], "definitions": [], "derivation": [], "formalization_refs": [], "mechanism": "The argument reconstructs Popper's distinction between the logical status of a theory (which cannot be probabilified) and the methodological rule of preference (which maximizes informational content). It posits that preferring a severely tested theory is equivalent to preferring the theory that has survived the hardest attempts to kill it, thereby offering the highest potential for learning if it is eventually false.
